3.0.0.en: 1 After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him. 2 And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence. 3 Then the king’s servants, which were in the king’s gate, said unto Mordecai, “Why transgressest thou the king’s commandment?” 4 Now it came to pass, when they spake daily unto him, and he hearkened not unto them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai’s matters would stand: for he had told them that he was a Jew. 5 And when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath. 6 And he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai.

3.0.1.en: “Haman” is the name of one of the chief gods in Elam, which the kingdom of Media and Persia took possession of and made one of its states, and it made its capital “Shushan” or “Susa” a capital where the kings of Persia stayed in the winter.

3.0.2.en: Haman the Agagite came from the descendants of Amalek (1 Sam 15:3, 9), whom Saul treated lightly and did not utterly destroy, so there came from them one who almost exterminated the whole people in one day. Thus Haman represents the sin that man makes light of and is careless in uprooting, so that his whole life is exposed to danger at the opportune moment.

3.0.3.en: “After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him. And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman” [1-2].

3.1.0.en: Haman had received great honor above all, so he became great in his own eyes, and wanted everyone to submit to him and bow down in worship of him. It is as though he bears the spirit of his master, the devil, who wanted to set himself up as a god. Therefore when Mordecai the Jew refused to bow to him [2], “Haman was full of wrath” [5], “and he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai” [6].

3.2.0.en: It is true that the Jews were accustomed to bow down before their kings as a mark of honor (2 Sam 14:4; 18:28; 1 Kgs 1:16), but the Persians offered worship to their kings, so the believers refused to take part with them in this act. And when Mordecai was asked about his not bowing down, “he had told them that he was a Jew” [4], and it was not permitted for him to take part with them in this act.

3.2.1.en: It is not strange that Haman should demand the extermination of all the people, for since he represents the devil while Mordecai is a type of the Lord Christ, the enemy of good cannot bear the people of Christ, who are the Kingdom of God.

3.2.2.en: Here we pause a little to see Mordecai as a type of the Lord Christ, because of whom Haman (the devil) wanted to exterminate all His people. Father Aphrahat says that just as Mordecai was persecuted by wicked Haman, so the wicked people persecuted the Lord Christ. And as Mordecai prayed for his people to save them from Haman, the Lord Christ intercedes for His people (by His blood) to save them from the devil. And as Mordecai was saved from his persecutor, the persecutors were unable to triumph over the Lord Christ. And as Mordecai sat in sackcloth and rescued his people, so the Word of God came down and took our body as in sackcloth and in humility saved us. Through Mordecai Esther became pleasing to the king instead of Vashti, and through Christ Jesus the Church of the New Testament became the object of the Father’s pleasure instead of the Jewish synagogue. And as Mordecai urged Esther to fast with her maidens, so the Lord Christ urges His Church with all her children to fast. Finally Mordecai received Haman’s glory, and it was proclaimed before him: [Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour] (Esth 6:11); and as for Jesus Christ, He was glorified with the glory that was His from eternity, and the guards bore witness to Him: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mt 27:54).

3.2.3.en: Haman discovered that what Mordecai was doing was not based on personal enmity but on a spiritual foundation of piety, so he thought there was no remedy for this problem except the extermination of the whole people.

3.2.4.en: St. Jerome sees that the word “Haman” means (unjustly). Now when the flames of injustice are kindled into wrath, they only burn themselves, for he says: [Haman, which means (unjustly), was burned with the fire that he himself kindled].

3.2.5.en: Here it is fitting for us to affirm that what Mordecai did in not bowing down to Haman was not out of hatred or enmity within his heart, nor out of pride, but as he said in his prayer found in the Additions to Esther: “Thou knowest all things, and knowest that it was not out of pride, nor contempt, nor desire for any honor that I did this, that I did not bow down to the arrogant Haman. For I am ready to kiss even the traces of his feet with a willing mind for the deliverance of Israel, but I feared to turn the honor of my God to a man and to worship anyone but my God” (Additions to Esth 13:12-14).

3.2.6.en: He does not disdain to kiss the traces of Haman’s feet for the salvation of his brethren; thus his heart is enlarged with love and filled with humility, but he does not accept to worship any but God!

3.3.0.en: 7 In the first month, that is, the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, before Haman from day to day, and from month to month, to the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar. 8 And Haman said unto king Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king’s laws: therefore it is not fitting for the king to suffer them. 9 If it please the king, let it be written that they may be destroyed: and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the hands of those that have the charge of the business, to bring it into the king’s treasuries.” 10 And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews’ enemy. 11 And the king said unto Haman, “The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee.” 12 Then were the king’s scribes called on the thirteenth day of the first month, and there was written according to all that Haman had commanded unto the king’s lieutenants, and to the governors that were over every province, and to the rulers of every people of every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language; in the name of king Ahasuerus was it written, and sealed with the king’s ring. 13 And the letters were sent by posts into all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews, both young and old, little children and women, in one day, even upon the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to take the spoil of them for a prey. 14 The copy of the writing for a commandment to be given in every province was published unto all people, that they should be ready against that day.

3.3.1.en: Since Haman counted the insult that came to him from Mordecai as not atoned for by the killing of one person, he demanded the extermination of the whole Jewish people. So in April of the year 474 B.C., that is, about 4 years after Esther’s coronation, Haman asked the diviners and magicians to cast Pur, that is, a lot, so as to determine the proper day for exterminating this people so that his plan would not fail. They fixed it on the thirteenth day of the last month of the year (the month of Adar), and thus gave him a long and sufficient respite to accomplish his purpose in one day in all parts of the kingdom.

3.3.2.en: Haman met the king and incited him against the people by accusing them of being breakers of the laws who deserve nothing but extermination, and he offered ten thousand talents of silver as the price of this work. As we have said, he wanted to gather the wealth of all the Jews, so that he would become rich and offer this sum to the king, perhaps to compensate him for his losses a few years earlier in his war against Greece, or in return for his losses of the tribute that the Jews used to pay. For the Jews were known for exaggerated wealth even in the land of captivity; in recent discoveries many Jewish names have been found performing the work of money-changers in the region of Babylon in the period of the captivity.

3.4.0.en: The king handed his ring to Haman, and said to him: “The silver... is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee” [11]. Thus the king trusted Haman and loved him so much that he handed him the ring to write what he wished; even the silver that Haman offered to give the king as compensation he waived to him, and as for the whole people, they were in his hands to do with as he wished... And indeed “the letters were sent by posts into all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews, both young and old, little children and women, in one day, even upon the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to take the spoil of them for a prey” [13]. It is a faint picture of the sentence that was passed on us because of the envy of Haman (the devil), so that all without exception came under the sentence of death, so that everyone who looks at himself makes great mourning and weeps day and night (Esth 4:3). And as the Apostle says: “Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” (Rom 5:12).

3.4.1.en: This bitter sentence turns against Haman and his followers through Mordecai and Esther and becomes salvation, joy and a feast for all the people. Thus if through the devil we fell under the sentence of death, then through Christ Jesus (the true Mordecai) Esther and her people (the Church) enjoyed salvation, joy and the heavenly feast, while the devil and all his soldiers collapsed beneath the Cross. As the Apostle says: “Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:14-15).

3.5.s.en: 3. The king and Haman sit down to drink:

3.5.0.en: 15 The posts went out, being hastened by the king’s commandment, and the decree was given in Shushan the palace. And the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed.

3.5.1.en: The king had only one ear, with which he listened to Haman without inquiring about the other side. He did not examine the matter himself but handed everything over into Haman’s hand. And since Haman feared lest the king retract and realize the matter, he drank with him, so that the king would be distracted by his pleasures at the expense of his people.

3.5.2.en: The “Additions to Esther” found in the Septuagint present to us a copy of the royal decree sent in the name of Ahasuerus, addressed to all the states or the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and it agreed with the conversation mentioned in this chapter between Haman and the king. The most important of what it contained:

3.5.3.en: First: the Jews were accused of ingratitude, as people to whom the king does good and who repay the kindness by violating the laws, and he considered that their destruction brings peace to all the lands, for he says: “so that when those wicked people go down to hell in one day, the peace which they disturbed may be restored to our kingdom” (Additions to Esth 13:7).

3.5.4.en: Second: Haman was called the second man after the king, and the king honors him as a father, so all are obliged to follow his counsel concerning the extermination of this enemy people, they and their wives and their children. Here we pause a little at the calling of Haman “a father,” for he represents the devil, who offers his followers an evil fatherhood, as the Lord Christ said to the wicked Jews: “Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do” (Jn 8:44). Just as God offers us His fatherhood, so that we bear as sons the characteristics of our Father and enjoy the fellowship of His eternal glory, so the enemy of good, the devil, offers his fatherhood to his followers that they may bear his characteristics and share his eternal destruction.

4.0.0.en: “1 When Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and a bitter cry; 2 And came even before the king’s gate: for none might enter into the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth. 3 And in every province, whithersoever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.” [1-3].

4.0.1.en: When Mordecai learned what Haman had done, he rent his clothes as a sign of intense grief, as Reuben did when he returned to the pit and did not find Joseph his brother (Gen 37:29), and he put on sackcloth as a sign of the contrition of his heart and his humbling, and cried with a bitter cry, for he realized that what had befallen his people was because of him... Moreover Mordecai enjoyed a heart enlarged with love for his brethren, so he could not bear to see their sufferings. He is like Nehemiah, who heard the grievous news in Jerusalem and said: “I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven” (Neh 1:4). And the Apostle Paul bore the same heart when he said: [I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh] (Rom 9:1-3).

4.0.2.en: If Mordecai represents the Lord Christ, then the way of salvation began with Mordecai’s rending his clothes, putting on sackcloth, and going out into the city to cry with a bitter cry that shakes the gates of heaven, so that Queen Esther and her people are saved from extermination. Thus the Lord Christ laid aside His glory, emptying Himself for our sake (the rending of the clothes), taking our body (putting on sackcloth), dwelling in our midst on our earth (his going out into the city), and cried on the Cross to give up His spirit for our salvation. As Father Aphrahat says: [When Mordecai sat and wrapped himself in sackcloth he rescued Esther and her people from the sword; since Christ put on a body... He saved the Church and her children from death].

4.0.3.en: In every province to which the king’s command came, the life of the Jews was turned into mourning, fasting and weeping, and many spread sackcloth, following the example of Mordecai... It is a living picture of the believers who contemplate the great Day of the Lord and, as they realize the work of sin within them, mourn, offering sincere repentance so as to seize the mercies of the Lord.

4.0.4.en: Finally Mordecai came before the king’s gate but did not enter because of the sackcloth. Thus the kings lived in their palaces, not wanting to meet the suffering and the wronged, caring for their own psychological comfort without concern for the people. They closed the doors before the one clothed in sackcloth, so that the King of kings Himself might come down clothed in sackcloth, and share their sufferings, and lead them by His Holy Spirit not to the king’s gate or inside his palace, but to the very bosom of the Father. Thus the great closed the doors of their palaces in the face of the needy, so that the Great One might come down to them and carry them to His heavens.

4.1.s.en: 2. Esther’s grief and her sending Hatach to him:

4.1.0.en: 4 So Esther’s maids and her chamberlains came and told it her. Then was the queen exceedingly grieved; and she sent raiment to clothe Mordecai, and to take away his sackcloth from him: but he received it not. 5 Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king’s chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was. 6 So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, which was before the king’s gate. 7 And Mordecai told him of all that had happened unto him, and of the sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them. 8 Also he gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given at Shushan to destroy them, to shew it unto Esther, and to declare it unto her, and to charge her that she should go in unto the king, to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people. 9 And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.

4.1.1.en: Esther was exceedingly grieved when she heard what Mordecai had done, and she sent him garments, but he did not accept to take his sackcloth off him. So she sent to him Hatach, one of the chamberlains who were in her attendance, and Mordecai told him all that Haman had done and gave him a copy of the king’s decree, and asked him to charge Esther to go in unto the king, and make supplication unto him, and make request of him for her people.

4.1.2.en: If Mordecai put on sackcloth in humbling himself before God, then in courage he declared his grief in the midst of the city and did not hide the bitterness of his soul; when the queen asked him to put on garments that she sent to him, he refused. She sent him Hatach, who seems to have been a Jew, since it is said of him in the second Targum that he had another name, “Daniel.” For this reason Mordecai spoke to him with complete frankness and asked him to declare the matter to Esther, that she might intervene by meeting with the king.

4.2.0.en: 10 Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment unto Mordecai; 11 “All the king’s servants, and the people of the king’s provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.” 12 And they told to Mordecai Esther’s words. 13 Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king’s house, more than all the Jews. 14 For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” 15 Then Esther bade them return Mordecai this answer, 16 “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.” 17 So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

4.3.0.en: When Hatach told Esther the words of Mordecai, she sent to him saying that she had not been called to go in to the king these thirty days, and if she went in she would be killed unless the king held out the golden sceptre, and then she would live. But he returned to tell her: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king’s house, more than all the Jews. For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” [13-14].

4.3.1.en: If Mordecai rent his clothes, put on sackcloth and cried with a bitter cry in the midst of the city, it was not out of despair or loss of hope but out of humbling himself before God, believing that He is able to act, and urging his people to share with him in contrition before God... This is what his words to Esther revealed, for he believed that salvation was surely coming, through Esther or through another, God works, for he says to her: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place.” It is as though he says to her: God does not lack the means; He will save in any case, but I fear that you will lose your crown, for perhaps He sent you to this place to work through you so that you may enjoy the crown.

4.3.2.en: Would that in the time of temptation we were like Mordecai, who believes that salvation is surely coming and that God will certainly rescue; yet would that we come out of the temptation conquerors and victorious, not broken and losers. If we believe in the work of God, the temptation ends and we have been crowned in His eyes, and we acquire for ourselves gain on a heavenly level.

4.3.3.en: Mordecai affirmed to Esther that the events of her life are not a collection of coincidences nor the fruit of purely human striving, but a divine plan for the glory of God, the building up of the Church and the growth of Esther’s spiritual life. So Joseph believed when he said to his brethren who had delivered him into slavery: “Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life” (Gen 45:5)... So if Esther has become queen or Joseph was sold as a slave, God, the Lord of history, brings them in to where they glorify Him on behalf of the whole holy community.

4.3.4.en: Mordecai revealed to her that she should come out of the circle of narrow thinking, and not think about her life or her death, because what befalls her people touches her life and the life of her father’s house, for he says to her: “Think not... that thou shalt escape in the king’s house.” At the same time he affirmed to her that the work she does is done by God Himself, for He will surely save; so if she stretches out her hand to the work, God Himself, as a Father, is committed to the work... so do not fear.

4.3.5.en: Would that we always work going forth from the circle of the ego, realizing that the spiritual work of God will not fail, and that His hand is able to save if we deliver our lives into His hands.

4.4.0.en: If Mordecai confronted Esther with frankness and courage to remove from her all fear, then in humility the queen received his message, and her answer revealed a heart enlarged with transcendent love, for she said: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish” [16].

4.4.1.en: Esther loved her people, so she offered her life to death for them: “if I perish, I perish.” Though she was a great queen, fair to look on, in the prime of her life, loved by her husband, she accepted to go in to him without his calling her, though she knew his savagery, which knows no mercy even toward his friends. For when Lysias begged him to spare his eldest son from the war, offering his other five sons, all he did was cut the boy in two and ask the soldiers to walk over his body with their feet, so that all would know his firmness and sternness.

4.4.2.en: She exposed her life to destruction by faith. She did not cast blame on Mordecai nor accuse him of pride for not submitting to Haman, but by a living faith realized that her own sins and those of all her people were the cause, for we hear in her prayer found in the Additions to Esther that she says: “And now we have sinned before thee, and thou hast delivered us into the hands of our enemies, because we worshipped their gods: O Lord, thou art righteous” (Additions to Esth 14:6-7)... By faith she knew the key of salvation: confession of sins and returning to God the Savior.

4.4.3.en: Esther did not think in a human, temporal way. She did not care how to adorn herself and perfume herself to attract the king, nor did she ask Mordecai to arrange a plot against Haman, but she knew that salvation is from God, so she resorted to fasting and prayer, and asked that Mordecai and all the other Jews who were in the city of Shushan (Susa) share with her, as her maids shared with her... And here we pause at her maids’ sharing with her in her fasting from eating and drinking three days and in her prayers, for in this is a revelation of Esther’s life with them. She lived with them not as one giving commands and prohibitions but as a mother caring for their salvation; they bore with her the spirit of piety and godliness, therefore they shared with her in her distress with fitting spiritual thought! Would that we cared even for servants, for we are responsible for their salvation as brethren to us who share with us membership in the one Body.

4.4.4.en: It was necessary for Esther to go in to the king, but she wanted to enter into his heart by God, in whose hand alone is the king’s heart (Prov 21:1). So she resorted to Him by fasting and prayer, that He might change his stony nature and open his doors to her, so that she would enter with the Lord Himself to save her with her people. In this St. Ambrose says: [Esther by her fasts moved the arrogant king]. And St. Clement of Rome says: [Esther, who was perfect in faith, exposed herself to a danger no less (than Judith), to rescue the twelve tribes of Israel from certain destruction. For she besought by fasting and humility the everlasting God who sees all things, and He, seeing the humility of her spirit, saved the people for whose sake she had exposed herself to death]. And it is stated in the book (the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles): “By fasting Esther, Mordecai and Judith escaped the plots of the wicked Holofernes and Haman.”

4.4.5.en: With perfect love for her people and perfect trust in God, who works in the lives of the humble, Esther fasted and went forth with courage to the work, saying: “if I perish, I perish,” not out of unbelief in God’s salvation, but out of love, ready to perish that the people might live, and to die for her brethren. And as St. Ambrose says: [Why did Esther expose her life to death and not fear the wrath of the savage king? Was it not to save her people from death, a fitting matter filled with virtue!].

4.4.6.en: Esther bore the spirit of the three youths who said: “If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not (even if we die bodily), be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:17-18).

4.4.7.en: She asked for an absolute fast from all eating and drinking for three days, as though she wanted to enter with the Lord into His tomb in order to rise with Him on the third day. She believed in Him who is able to raise her and her people from death. It is as though she shared with Jonah, the type of Christ, and entered into the belly of the whale, beholding the burial of the Lord Christ and His bearing death for His people, in order to come forth preaching the good tidings of life.

4.4.8.en: It is stated in the Additions to Esther (Additions to Esth 14) that she took off the royal garments and put on garments of grief and weeping, and instead of the various perfumes she cast ashes on her head, and humbled her body with fasting, and she tore out the hair of her head, and stood supplicating God, confessing her sins and those of her people, reminding Him of His promises and His works with her fathers, and asking Him to look upon the humiliation of His people and their distress at the hands of the pagans.

4.4.9.en: Esther believed that it is God who speaks through her mouth so that the words would pierce the heart of this savage lion, for she said: “Put eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion, and turn his heart to hate our enemy, that there may be an end of him and of all that are likeminded to him.” (Additions to Esth 14:13). For she does not capture the king’s heart by her beauty or her coquetry or her own wisdom, but by God, who speaks in her mouth and works in the heart of this lion. St. John Chrysostom says: [Esther rescued the whole people of the Jews when it was about to perish utterly, by using this means (prayer)...! She asked the merciful God to go with her to the king, and offered Him her prayers, when she said: “Put in my mouth acceptable speech...”].

4.4.10.en: In her prayer Esther revealed her inner life. She lived as a great queen possessing glory and honor, yet her heart was exceedingly simple, nothing of the honor of this world and its pleasures entering it. As she said: “Thou knowest my necessity: that I abhor the sign of my high estate, which is upon mine head in the days wherein I shew myself, and that I abhor it as a menstruous rag, and that I wear it not when I am private by myself. And that thine handmaid hath not eaten at Haman’s table, and that I have not delighted in the king’s feast, nor drunk the wine of the drink offerings. Neither hath thine handmaid had any joy since the day that I was brought hither to this present, but in thee, O Lord God of Abraham” (Additions to Esth 14:16-18).

4.4.11.en: Thus she lived in the palace as a queen, but she realized that she was a captive woman; her crown in her eyes was like a menstruous rag, she did not desire it but found it burdensome. She did not eat with Haman, the second man after the king, nor did she find pleasure in the king’s table, nor did she share in drinking the wine offered as a libation to the gods, and none gladdened her except the God of Abraham!

4.4.12.en: And this explains to us how, when she went in to the king before her selection, “she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain appointed” (Esth 2:15), since her heart was not attached to anything, even the crown of the kingdom!

4.4.13.en: St. Augustine presented Esther to us as an example for those who are in office and have high and great positions and are busy in public affairs, but whose hearts are open to heaven, for he says: [Of this kind is the holy lady Esther, who, although she was the king’s wife, exposed her life to danger interceding for her people; when she prayed, she said that the royal adornment was to her like a menstruous rag].

4.4.14.en: And when St. Jerome praised one of the women recently consecrated to the Lord, he said: [She came to hate every splendid garment, and cried out to the Lord like Esther: “Thou knowest my necessity, that I abhor the sign of my high estate and my glory (that is, the crown she wore as queen), and I abhor it as a menstruous rag”].
